Breaking: Pedro Almodóvar Didn’t Think He Could Write a Novel. But Once He Started, the “Story Began to Pour Out”

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A woman who might, or might not, be Penélope Cruz stares down at us from the wall.
  • In a recent development, this brings to mind one of the stories in Almodóvar’s first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes.
  • According to recent reports, both works have much in common: They are works of autofiction with protagonists—the filmmakers played by Bárbara Lennie and Leonardo Sbaraglia in the film, and a very multifaceted character named Flavio Guijarro in the book—who appear to be alternative versions of their creator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A woman who might, or might not, be Penélope Cruz stares down at us from the wall. For now, I’ll accept that it is Cruz because the image is on a poster for Broken Embraces, a 2009 film she starred in. My hesitation in believing it’s her, however, is because finding a resemblance between the woman on the poster and Cruz requires a lot of generosity. It’s as if the artist had painted her based on a detailed description he’d heard, but he’d never actually seen his subject onscreen. “We were given this in India,” explains Pedro Almodóvar’s brother, Agustín, the head and owner of El Deseo, the production firm behind Almodóvar’s films. “Specialized artists still hand-paint their movie posters, and the results are images like this.” The work’s imperfections give it a charm that no poster created by AI could ever match.

In a recent development, this brings to mind one of the stories in Almodóvar’s first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes. It depicts a Blade Runner–style dystopian future where replicants, jaded by digital perfection, are fascinated by the rough edges of human culture. The book has just been published in Spain (it is scheduled to be published in the United States, in Spanish, in February 2027), following the release of Almodóvar’s latest film, Bitter Christmas (which will be in select US theaters on November 13, and released nationwide on November 25).

According to recent reports, both works have much in common: They are works of autofiction with protagonists—the filmmakers played by Bárbara Lennie and Leonardo Sbaraglia in the film, and a very multifaceted character named Flavio Guijarro in the book—who appear to be alternative versions of their creator. At the same time, they are clearly different from Almodóvar, like the difference between Cruz and the woman on the Indian movie poster.

Sources indicate that I ask Almodóvar why he decided to recount Flavio’s story in the form of a novel rather than a movie, but he appears to have not heard my question and answers instead as if I’d asked him why it took him so long to publish a novel, which is undoubtedly much more interesting: “I think the reason I hadn’t written a novel until now was that I wasn’t sure I’d be able to, even though I’d wanted to write one since I was a young man. At first, however, I didn’t even know myself that this story would be a novel. I started with a simple anecdote about an acting coach and an actor, and that opened the floodgates; the story began to pour out. When it was already over 30 pages, I sent it to my editor. He told me there was a novel there and that I should keep going.”.

The 77-year-old director from La Mancha poses in a jacket, polo shirt, pants, and sneakers by Loewe.

It has been revealed that he will answer many other questions that I haven’t asked but should have: “I didn’t know, for example, that I’d include my story ‘Addiction,’ which is a little treat for fans that had already appeared in Pain and Glory. It was going to be a monologue that Carmen Machi would perform in a small theater, but I ended up giving it to Asier Etxeandia in that film. I also wrote Pain and Glory very promptly. And in it, I inserted, like little snippets, more pieces that I’d already written. For example, there’s another story, just five pages long, about a chance encounter with an actor with whom I’d had a very bad relationship in the past [Eusebio Poncela, who starred in Law of Desire 40 years ago] and with whom, in the story, I ended up doing heroin. In real life, the fact that he was using heroin while we were filming was the reason we had a falling out. Thanks to those preexisting elements, which fit into the story, I was able to write that movie so quickly. And the same is true of my latest book. What defines it is a sense of absolute freedom.”.

And maybe that sentence is, in the end, the answer to all my questions for Almodóvar.

Vanity Fair España: Is that sense of freedom why you decided to write a novel instead of a screenplay?

According to recent reports, pedro Almodóvar: In Bitter Christmas, Leonardo Sbaraglia’s character states he needs absolute freedom to work. Just like me throughout my entire career. That freedom feels more intense with a novel because it’s a format with which I have less experience. I’ve woven it together from different stories, but they all revolve around the protagonist and it’s been very satisfying. It wasn’t a whim: The book has the same rigor to it as everything else I do, but that freedom is deeply rooted in my style. That’s why I wrote it so swiftly. Everything flowed naturally.

There is a tradition of using a novel as a container for many stories, as with Don Quixote or Jan Potocki’s The Manuscript Found in Saragossa. On the other hand, speaking of influences, it’s interesting that when you wrote your Patty Diphusa stories in 1983 [included in Patty Diphusa and Other Writings, published by Faber & Faber in 1992], Anita Loos and pornographic photo novels are influences that appear in the mix, but in The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes, you turn to, let’s say, more distinguished names: Henry James, Nabokov, and Colm Tóibín, who even appears as a character.

Sources indicate that I’m not trying to compare myself to Cervantes or Potocki, but yes, that’s what the book is. That’s precisely why this novel can’t be adapted for the screen: You’d have to choose one part of it and develop it, but as it stands now, that wouldn’t be possible. Those earlier influences are still with me—Anita Loos is certainly among them—and they continue to inspire me with both specific phrases and broader themes. In the novel, I name authors who inspire me and with whom I connect organically, such as Joan Didion and Virginia Woolf. But Patty and Flavio have something in common: a sense of urgency that drives them to write at a breakneck pace, out of a physiological need. Neither of them sleeps much, though in Patty’s case it’s because she can’t stop doing cocaine. Beyond that, other differences set them apart, including the differences between what life was like in the ’80s and what it’s like now.

What sort of differences are there, and where are they most apparent?

Take sex, for example. Patty Diphusa is an archetype of the 1980s, a time of absolute freedom in Spain, and her character can only be understood in the context of the utterly carefree and hedonistic lifestyle we led back then. If she sucks a guy's dick in a bathroom, she’ll then record her wild thoughts because she considers herself a sort of philosopher of eroticism. Although Flavio is a very free-spirited person, just like the book itself, he belongs to another era and another generation. Here, sex is part of a love story, and his attitude toward it is very different. I devote less space to the erotic scenes in this book because I assume people already know what it’s like to sleep with someone.

Almodóvar, in another room at El Deseo’s headquarters, wearing a Louis Vuitton jacket and a Prada knit polo shirt.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve argued on different occasions that in the 1980s, many people in Spain chose that hedonistic and seemingly frivolous lifestyle as a reaction to the previous era, and that this was a political statement. Now we see a fresh generation adopting a different kind of stance. For example, all across Europe, people are taking to the streets to demand their right to housing and decent living conditions, and there’s not much frivolity in that. How do you interpret this change?

It has been revealed that I completely empathize with and support the people filling the streets. They are demanding fundamental rights that are enshrined in the Spanish constitution and which are now in jeopardy: housing, health care, and education. I went to the encampment on the Puerta del Sol [in Madrid] only a few times, because I was in Latest York presenting Bitter Christmas at the New York Film Festival and also because I think a famous person doesn’t really fit in at these demonstrations—if we go, we distort the spirit of it. But I did go, and I bought them food because that’s what I thought they’d need, even though they told me they’d be better off with some tables. I don’t just support their initiative; I’m glad it happened. One thing I’d heard about young people, a generation I don’t know much about, was from a news article that said that 25% of young Spaniards wouldn’t mind living under a dictatorship like Franco’s. I shuddered. What happened in the Puerta del Sol reveals that there’s a whole crowd of young people beyond those who go to Ferraz to pray the rosary [since November 2023, a group of Catholic protesters has gathered daily to pray outside the headquarters of the PSOE, Spain’s socialist party, on Madrid’s Calle Ferraz]. They aren’t rich, and they don’t have their lives figured out; they can’t work in the professions they studied to pursue, and they don’t earn enough money to buy homes. That’s terrifying. And the political parties have shown their true colors when it comes to housing. Of course, the PSOE is late to the game with the so-called Maricarmen decrees [a series of measures named after Maricarmen Abascal, whose eviction from her home and subsequent death in October galvanized activists], but at least it has reacted. The starkly different reactions from the Partido Popular [Popular Party] and Vox [center-right and far-right parties, respectively] already tell you what they think about this concern.

Would you agree today with that line from Gloria Muñoz in The Flower of My Secret: “With so much reality, the country’s ready to explode”?

She was talking in literary terms, but it’s true that this phrase has taken on a life of its own over time and has spilled over into other areas. The same thing has happened to another phrase: “A woman is more authentic the more she resembles the person she has dreamed of becoming,” as Agrado mentioned in All About My Mother. It was a line written for a transgender woman, and one that makes perfect sense for her. But now it can be understood in relation to any kind of character: It speaks to authenticity, to staying true to oneself and to one’s own dreams. In the case of young people in our country, we’re talking about a social reality. The country has changed a lot, and we’re very polarized—though France is even worse off than Spain. Europe is in very bad shape overall. The kind of news coverage being produced plays a major role in this rise of the far right. Since the images promoted by the right are so jarring and sensationalist, TV stations pick up on them, and in doing so, they’re effectively promoting figures like Vito Quiles [a far-right activist and influencer]. Damn it, don’t put Vito Quiles on TV—it’s better if we don’t even know where he is or what he’s doing!

Are you particularly concerned about the attention that the far right is getting?

Recent findings suggest that people like [Santiago] Abascal [president of the Vox political party] and [Javier]Milei [president of Argentina] want to do away with the state. Milei, the biggest loudmouth of them all, even aims to destroy the state from within the state itself, which is diabolical. I cite Milei as an example because he claims so himself. And on top of that, people elect him for that very reason: He’s someone who has come to power democratically, just like [Donald] Trump. So we’re putting the tools of democracy in the hands of someone whose main goal is to destroy it. Furthermore, in a world so polarized—and with a far right that has no qualms about calling itself fascist—the emergence of AI creates a perfect storm.

One of the stories in your book is, in fact, a dystopian tale inspired by Blade Runner, in which large corporations with shadowy agendas seek to create a less human world. You have contributed so much to human creativity. Are you concerned about how that creativity is being taken over by AI?

It has been revealed that I’m always open to change. It’s necessary for society to move forward. But I think the encroachment of AI on human agency is terrible. They should start regulating it now. I’m concerned about the jobs it will replace and also the synthetic culture it will create. In fact, a synthetic culture based on data already exists, and it lacks a soul. The genesis of a screenplay must be human, because AI doesn’t have the sense of doubt, the patience, or the capacity for stories to build up layers of meaning, as in Talk to Her and Bad Education. We need a society that cares about culture, promotes it, and supports it, and not a soulless culture focused only on the immediate. I haven’t used AI creatively, nor do I really know how to. But I’m concerned that we’re now unable to tell whether an image is real or not, given the level of perfection this technology has reached. And moreover, behind it all are very powerful people who know no limits.

Sources indicate that on another topic, standards of beauty have changed, with cosmetic surgery and fillers now widely prevalent. For someone who places such importance on the expressions of actors that must also be a cause for concern.

Sources indicate that well, I wouldn’t mind if an actor in one of my movies had had plastic surgery. For example, I wouldn’t turn down Nicole Kidman for that reason—she’s not only a great actor, but she has also had plastic surgery, and she looks better than ever. Because, these days, actors who’ve had plastic surgery are part of the landscape. It’s so common that you no longer have to explain that a character has had it done; it’s accepted as a matter of course. What’s more, cosmetic surgery has advanced so much that high-profile figures who’ve had work done—like Donatella Versace, Lindsay Lohan, or Nicole Kidman herself—have completely erased the signs of their previous procedures with splendid results. [Editor’s note: Lindsay Lohan has denied having a facelift, while Kidman has never confirmed undergoing any plastic surgery.] The big problem is that, if you make films set in the past, you can’t cast women with plastic surgery or lip fillers; it would be anachronistic, just like putting a piece of furniture from the 1980s in a film about the Spanish Civil War. But it’s true that in my films, plastic surgery hasn’t usually been an option, for aesthetic reasons. Fortunately, there will always be people like Frances McDormand and Carmen Maura. We need older women who look their age.

What interests me most about your newly introduced novel is the protagonist’s relationship with an actor, Alez Mazado—a sex symbol who isn’t very intelligent but has a certain natural talent and is open to being molded. Flavio is his Pygmalion. There’s even an explicit reference to Hitchcock’s film Vertigo, which also features that kind of relationship. Do you often have that kind of dynamic with your actors?

Industry observers note that I’m like Jimmy Stewart in Vertigo: With actors, I get involved in their hair, lip color, outfits—everything. When I watched Vertigo for the umpteenth time, I thought that character was a director: “He knows exactly what he wants,” they tell him when he takes Kim Novak to try on outfits at a store. The actors I work with and I have adapted to each other, just like in a marriage—in my films, they speak differently; the actors themselves say so. Aitana Sánchez-Gijón told me that she felt she could do anything after playing her role in Bitter Christmas. But I work differently with each actor. With Penélope, for example, I rehearse a lot, and the more we rehearse, the better she gets; then I shoot many takes, and the 10th one is better than the third. And if I can shoot 12, even better. But others don’t like to rehearse, like Antonio Banderas, because he’s a different kind of actor. He has extraordinary intuition and instinct. I don’t need to talk to him as much or push him so hard.

People talk about Los Javis [the moniker for actors turned directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo] as your natural heirs, in the wake of the success of La Bola Negra, which you coproduced through El Deseo. Do you think they will continue your creative legacy?

They definitely treat me like their mentor. They know entire films of mine by heart, even lines that I don’t remember. They’ve been deeply influenced by my films, just as I’ve been influenced by [Luis García] Berlanga, [Rafael] Azcona, [Luis] Buñuel, and [Carlos] Saura. Even if you don’t want to admit it, everyone has role models. I find it flattering, but to say they’re my heirs is to minimize their work. They have a style all their own. In fact, if I were to write the screenplay for La Bola Negra, it would be very different. I don’t feel like their father. I take responsibility for my films and nothing else.

How do you view their film’s unstoppable run at the awards and at the box office?

Los Javis are the big thing right now. Their film is going to be the highest-grossing Spanish movie of all time, although I don’t remember how much The Last Torch Song (1957), starring Sara Montiel, made back in the day. At El Deseo, we’ve had two fantastic years—first with Oliver Laxe’s film [Sirāt], which we also coproduced, and now this one. And I hope the Javis can keep on going and make it through the rest of their promotional tour and then the awards season. From my experience as an Oscar nominee, I know the best moment isn’t when they call your name, but when the ceremony ends. That’s when your life is your own again—whether to start on the next project or simply sleep if that’s what you prefer.

According to recent reports, have you shared that experience with the Javis? Do you give them advice?

Just yesterday I texted Javier Ambrossi, and he told me they’ve already had enough. And they have no idea what’s still in store for them! We’ll meet next week, and I’ll explain it all to him. At the Oscars, they’re the favorites in the best-international-feature-film category; they’re a sure thing. Although I experienced that curse of being the front-runner when Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown was the favorite and then Pelle the Conqueror ended up winning—a film no one even remembers now. But anyway, everyone now expects La Bola Negra to be nominated in other categories as well, which is historic for our film industry. It’s great for us.

On a recent podcast, one of the actors from La Bola Negra, Yenesi, described the film as Federico García Lorca fan fiction—which is actually quite fitting, since its entire narrative is built on elements related to Lorca’s life and writings. Roland Barthes had already spoken of the death of the author, and Eugenio d’Ors famously said, “There is no true originality outside tradition. Everything that is not tradition is plagiarism.”.

According to recent reports, I’ve written that phrase down! I read it in one of [journalist and writer Francisco] Umbral’s columns; I suppose he got it from d’Ors.

In other words, Umbral appropriated it for himself, and in doing so, he proved its enduring relevance.

Recent findings suggest that it’s inevitable that the things you like will influence your work. And the things you hate too. When you write, you have a general idea of the story, but as you develop it, what you create is rooted in things that are part of your life. And your life always resembles the things you’ve seen before. I’m fascinated by the phenomenon of fan fiction because of its contradictory nature; it’s a miracle that an entire culture has developed around this phenomenon, which exists outside the mainstream market yet at the same time feeds off the most mainstream works, such as Star Trek or Star Wars. Fan fiction is a declaration of love for the original and proof that great stories never end: There will always be someone to continue them. Just as people don’t die as long as there’s someone who remembers them.

Of course I have to ask you, with the promotional tour for Bitter Christmas coming to an end, what are you working on next?

Industry observers note that well, it was going to be a comedy, but after I finished it, even though I was 90% passionate about it, I realized there was something about the supporting characters that I didn’t like. So I’ve put it on hold, as I’ve done before with other projects. And now I’m writing something else. I’m well into it, but I can’t say anything. They’ll kill me if I do. It’ll be based on a book, and we’re currently working out the rights. This one will have plenty of humor too. Because I know for sure that, after Bitter Christmas, I don’t want to talk about myself anymore. I need different characters. And humor too.

Is there any movie you wish you’d made but that’s missing from your filmography?

According to recent reports, there are several recent films I would have loved to have made. For example, Drive My Car by Ryusuke Hamaguchi and Anatomy of a Fall by Justine Triet. Or Sentimental Value by Joachim Trier. I mean, I should have made that movie! It has everything: the cinema, a house, a father and his daughters. Everything.

Should we just accept, by the way, that you won’t make your own movie about the Spanish Civil War? Or was Parallel Mothers already your take on it?

According to recent reports, when I read Cosamala, Alana S. Portero’s latest book, I really wanted to adapt it. But it’s such a wonderful work of literature that translating it into images would greatly diminish the wonder and surprise of her writing. If the book proves anything, it’s that Alana is a tremendous writer. I’d have to find another angle from which to tell the story of the civil war. But I do want to do it.

Jenny McCarthy is getting candid about her previously botched breast augmentation procedure.

According to recent reports, “This was back when I was living on the south side of Chicago and all of my girlfriends were going to Arizona to get this boob job that was on sale for $1,500,” McCarthy, 54, recalled on the Thursday, November 19, episode of her eponymous podcast. “They would come back with the most gorgeous freaking cleavage you’d ever seen. Growing up as an athlete and not having a lot of meat on my bones, I craved boobs.”.

Following in her friends’ footsteps, a then-19-year-old McCarthy “saved up” her money to get her own procedure.

“I go to Arizona, I do the appointment. He’s like, ‘OK.’ I tell him, ‘I just want small C’s just so they’re not that noticeable.’ I go in for the surgery. I’m very, very nervous,” she mentioned of the plastic surgeon. “Halfway through the surgery, I wake up on the table and I literally say to the doctor, ‘Um, I’m awake.’ And he goes, ‘Oh, yeah. Well, we’ve got just one more boob to go.’”.

McCarthy was admittedly “freaking out” that the anesthesia allegedly wore off before the second implant was even surgically placed in her chest.

“He’s like, ‘Just hang out, just chill. You’ll be fine.’ I remember him saying, “You won’t remember a thing.’ I remember everything, buddy,” she quipped. “Now I know why it was so cheap ‘cause they didn’t put us to sleep!”.

McCarthy continued, “During a boob job surgery, I had no idea they did this, but once they put the implants in, they press a button … and the table rises you up to a standing position, and all of the doctors and nurses go to the other side of the room and they go and they’re literally examining you from across the room to see if you’re even.”.

Since McCarthy was awake, the examination was especially terrifying.

According to recent reports, “Now, this would be fine if you’re asleep right now. Imagine you were me, OK? I’m standing there strapped to the table like this having these people stare at me to see if it’s even,” she mentioned. “I wanted to go home so bad. I’m like, ‘This was the biggest mistake of my life.’”.

An investigation into the workplace behavior of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned recently after a series of extramarital affairs came to light, has uncovered decades of harassment, verbal employee abuse and "cultish" behaviour at the company which has long played a major role in PC gaming.

Industry observers note that following Huang's departure, The Newly introduced York Times has published a report in which "more than a dozen" current and former Nvidia employees discussed their experiences with the former CEO. Speaking on conditions of anonymity, employees alleged Jensen Huang would verbally berate them, reportedly going as far as to say he'd rip their arms off, rip their heart out and stomp on it, or rip their head off and "pee on your brain".

According to recent reports, the report includes numerous examples of Huang's alleged abusive behaviour, which apparently stretches back years before Nvidia became the one of the most valuable companies in the world - years before the AI boom. It's claimed Huang on one occasion went around a room of managers telling them he'd kill them. Then, when he reached a person in their 70s, said everyone hoped they'd drop dead.

It has been revealed that huang allegedly referred to these bouts of public humiliation as a "rite of passage" at Nvidia, when questioned by an internal HR employee whom he later fired for not being a "right fit". Huan's stance was apparently to test whether a person could handle the culture there, which is described in the report as "cultish".

It's claimed Huang's influence at Nvidia has meant other senior managers have followed his lead, including his daughter Madison, Nvidia's chief of staff, who it's stated often yells at staff, including executives more highly ranked than her.

A spokesperson for Huang denied the allegations in response to a request for comment by the New York Times. The spokesperson, John Fisher, said the claims in the report were "fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false".

According to recent reports, huang resigned from his role as Nvidia CEO earlier this month after a series of extramarital affairs were unearthed - one with a person US intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy, and two others with Nvidia employees. The chair of Nvidia's board, Harvey C. Jones, reportedly mentioned earlier this week that the manufacturer "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO".

Use of generative AI in game dev remains as contentious as it does ubiquitous—a recent GDC report found that around 40% of devs use AI, but more than half think its influence has been negative. Ubisoft is continuing to double down on the technology, this time with Motherbrain, a newly introduced subsidiary fashioned from the team behind its "first playable generative AI experience.".

As reported by VGC, Motherbrain's purpose is to develop "AI for gameplay innovation, supporting all game creators in developing groundbreaking experiences … Its current focus is on new player experiences, smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large scale systemic worlds," according to an earnings report which was released Thursday.

The information comes at a turbulent time for the publishing giant, which just laid off 166 employees even after Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced "outperformed expectations." A sweeping internal overhaul earlier this year saw the company reorganize its workforce into a throng of "creative houses," a decision which led to swathes of layoffs and six project cancellations, including the Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time Remake.

According to recent reports, it's not clear what Motherbrain are at work on, in specific terms, right now, but there may be some clues in its past work. That playable AI "experience" I mentioned earlier is none other than Teammates, an R&D project based on a prior experiment with uncanny AI "neo-NPCs.".

Teammates aimed to allow players to command NPC squadmates in a rudimentary shooter game with a microphone, and using AI, have those squadmates react believably. It's not far off, at least conceptually, from what we've seen in games like Where Winds Meet and Fortnite, both of which have experimented with AI-powered NPCs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest Apple Watches have a lot of latest features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks.
  • Industry observers note that the Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models.
  • You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of latest features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

Industry observers note that the Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is at the moment in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

Sources indicate that it's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own crucial details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

According to recent reports, first, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

In a recent development, if you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

According to recent reports, A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the fresh AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri releases into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

It has been revealed that if you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

He was a lovely houseguest, and a cheap date. He drank tap water. And he’s welcome back any time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ask a large language model the same question twice, and you will get two different answers. Like this one: Have Andrew Garfield and Sam Altman ever met?

In an interview with Vanity Fair global editorial director Mark Guiducci this fall, Altman claimed he waved to Garfield while Garfield was shooting Luca Guadagnino’s fresh film, Artificial, near Altman’s house. Garfield—who plays Altman in the movie—remembers things differently.

According to recent reports, “All I know is that I was looking out for him on that day when we were shooting. I was really looking out for him,” Garfield tells me in October, shortly after Artificial’s premiere at the Fresh York Film Festival. “And I was looking at every single tinted car window. I was looking in the windows of the house. I was checking to see the security guard. No, I didn’t see him. I wish I had.”.

According to recent reports, it’s a question that reverberates both through and around Artificial. From the start, the film has been an intriguing mash-up: a marriage between cinema’s great sensualist and the nerd kingdom of Silicon Valley. Artificial tells the story of the OpenAI CEO’s rise and fall and rise; it was cast and shot in record time to keep pace with the drumbeat of AI doomsday headlines. Then the movie became the headlines after Amazon MGM abruptly dropped Artificial from its slate—a few months after the studio’s parent tech giant, Amazon, invested $50 billion in OpenAI.

A24 declined to rescue Artificial. So did Netflix, Focus Features, and Clockwork, the latest specialty arm of Warner Bros. Finally, the lightning bolt of a feature got picked up by Neon, the distributor that’s won six consecutive Palmes d’Or at Cannes.

It has been revealed that the film’s electric relationship to the very recent past makes it the most zeitgeist-nailing tech blockbuster since The Social Network. The difference is that back in 2010, Facebook was where you made friends on the internet. Artificial, by contrast, is a film about a self-teaching, self-aware robot that’s getting smarter by the minute and might destroy the human world. And it’s happening in real time.

It has been revealed that “You see, we were very prescient with things,” Guadagnino tells me. “I know my subject. I studied my subject very, very much.”.

HERE TO MAKE FRIENDS Artificial ends with a heartbreaking act of betrayal—but Guadagnino, Borisov, and Garfield left the project with their bond intact.

It has been revealed that artificial also has a button-pushing relationship with the truth as it endeavors to tell the real story of how OpenAI was born and investigate how reliable the people behind OpenAI are. If Altman can’t be trusted with small details—about, say, whether he ever aimed a friendly wave at Garfield—can he be trusted with the most vital technology of our time?

Sources indicate that “I question the validity of his statement about being there while we were filming,” Monica Barbaro, who plays former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati in the film, tells me. “I mean, we don’t know if that’s true. And that feels textbook to me.”.

Sources indicate that in 2024, Amazon bought a script by Simon Rich about Sam Altman and the formation of OpenAI—one of many ChatGPT-related projects then getting passed around town. Rich’s take had the backing of hit-churning producer David Heyman—the man behind Paddington and the Harry Potter series—and his script pulled no punches. To write it, Rich mined details from a childhood friend who had a job at OpenAI (and, as of now, still works there). By the end of the process, Rich was terrified of the power his friend’s colleagues commanded.

Sources indicate that “I came up with this last-ditch effort to warn mankind,” Rich noted. He’s a comedy writer, but here he isn’t joking. “And I hope to God that it helps people pay attention.”.

Recent findings suggest that after shopping the film around to directors, the studio landed on Guadagnino. To some, the Call Me by Your Name director seemed like a strange choice for a film about scientists, coders, and start-up bros. The director barely uses AI himself, or even thinks about it.

ARTIFICIAL RECKONING Garfield’s first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network.

According to recent reports, “I think we should not let ourselves give AI such an notable role. I think for me, AI is a prop, a gadget,” Guadagnino tells me. “Definitely AI has high-end worth [for], I don’t know, the military, medicine. But in general, as a sort of everyday life usage of AI, I think it’s just a little gadget. And I don’t believe that we should ever consider the possibility that it can equal whatever we can do as people.”.

Industry observers note that garfield approached the material from a different vantage. By the time he got his hands on the script, the actor had been deeply invested in the Silicon Valley origin-story mythos for years—ever since he starred in that other major movie about a world-changing digital platform. His first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network. “And I thought, Oh my God,” notes the actor, sitting in a suite at the Carlyle Hotel. But the movie also had its own gloss. “Simon’s script was so funny—like a stone being skimmed a thousand times across, and then a couple of really deep dives in the midst.”.

Making Artificial would allow Garfield to scratch an old itch. “In The Social Network, I was auditioning for [Mark] Zuckerberg. Then they found Jesse [Eisenberg],” who was much better for the role, Garfield says. “But it left this little dangling thread, because I started to imagine how I would play Zuckerberg: how I would try and enter that ambition and that drive and that responsibility. A kind of ability to make huge global decisions that are going to have potentially really positive effects on humanity, but inevitably, really, really heavily negative effects on humanity.”.

THE ENGINEER “I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews,” states Borisov.

Garfield is not actually the lead in Artificial. The movie is focused less on Altman than on slightly naive genius coder Ilya Sutskever, played heroically by Oscar nominee Yura Borisov. Borisov has definitively never met the man he’s depicting in the film. But from afar, he can relate to Sutskever. Neither of them is quite comfortable in the spotlight.

“I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews because I’m every time very...I know what to say because I feel a lot about this,” the Russian actor says from a couch at the Carlyle next to Garfield. “I can see the same in his public speeches, because I’m really nervous during some public stuff.”.

In a recent development, though there’s a translator next to him, Borisov soldiers through the interview with just one request for a lifeline. He adds that by cosmic coincidence, he and Sutskever have the same birthday.

Guadagnino was fully aware of the breakneck clip of the developing OpenAI saga. He cast his leads in days and began shooting the film in late July 2025. Artificial wrapped just two months later. As he spent the winter hunkered down in the editing room, word about the film got out. While Rich’s original script was hardly a puff piece, rumor had it that the final film leaned even harder into a negative portrayal of Altman.

There’s no proof that a Jeff Bezos deal had any direct effect on decisions made by Bezos’s movie studio. But for whatever reason, late last spring, Guadagnino learned Amazon would be cutting the film loose.

All of a sudden, the speedily assembled project was in a holding pattern. The trades speculated that Amazon was deliberately killing the film to protect Altman; others wondered if the movie was being dropped not due to a conflict of interest but because it hadn’t played well in early screenings.

It has been revealed that barbaro pushes back on that notion. “I did believe in Luca and the film, and I had already heard really positive things from people who had seen it—really interesting positive reviews,” she says. “There is a thing these companies can do—any production firm—which is to essentially build the release and squash a film. And Amazon is not a company that I think necessarily needs to make its money back on an investment like this.”.

Either way, it was unclear if Artificial would ever see the light of day. “It’s a dialogue between our fields: tech and art,” Borisov indicates. “And I don’t know what sells, what will happen. It’s unpredictable.”.

In the end, the film was picked up by Neon—an outcome Garfield finds surprising for a few reasons. “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film, and very impressed again when they decided [that while] they didn’t want to release it, they didn’t kill it,” he says. He pauses for a second. “They could have killed it.”.

It has been revealed that garfield’s thrilled about the film’s eventual home too. Neon, he says pointedly, is “a place for artists to be free artists.” Guadagnino feels similarly, though he claims to have zero ill will toward the studio that threw his movie to the wolves.

“I had went through a process with Amazon that I loved. They were fantastic in making this movie with me. I owe them a lot,” says Guadagnino, who’d done four films with the studio prior to Artificial: Bones and All, Challengers, Suspiria, and After the Hunt.

But what was it like to watch his film fall into limbo while the trades salivated over its demise? Here too, Guadagnino is blissfully zen: “Once the thing happened, I deferred to the thing. Meaning if that was the case, that was the case.”.

Sources indicate that even after watching the film twice, I am still pleasantly surprised that Artificial actually exists in the world—that Guadagnino was able to capture the man-child bonhomie of coder bros through his fabulous scrim of art film wooziness. I ask Garfield, now a two-time vet of the director’s films, to sum up the full Guadagnino psychedelic experience.

“Humanity and bodies and interpersonal dynamics and relationship and sexuality, sensuality, Eros, love, the muck and the mire of being human, ambition, drive, greed, power, love, brotherhood, connection,” he indicates. Guadagnino’s movies are about “his curiosity and love for people: wanting to skin, flay, open up, crack the ribs, and show the insides of these human beings.”.

Sources indicate that to Garfield this is the key to understanding the director’s vision for Artificial. Robots didn’t build the robots that might destroy humanity: People did. And people still control them—for now.

It has been revealed that artificial inspires a lot of comparisons. Barbaro likens it to Invasion of the Body Snatchers; Garfield compares its climactic confrontation scene to West Side Story. Guadagnino, the actor states, gave another point of reference. Then he does a spot-on, peak-Sicilian impression of the director: “I want this to be like a John Hughes movie.”.

Industry observers note that guadagnino himself is reluctant to name any films that may have inspired this one. But he does name one filmmaker—someone who, as he notes, balanced indie flicks with blockbusters all while building the world’s greatest collection of Haitian art: Jonathan Demme.

Sources indicate that “Jonathan was a humanist, and he had this very profound capacity of eviscerating dynamics of humanism in America,” Guadagnino says. “He did some great movies about the dynamics of corporations versus individual freedom,” like Fighting Mad and Philadelphia.

Barbaro states the film’s secret sauce is that it’s up for interpretation. It’s possible to come away from it celebrating the AI bros as heroes or decrying them as villains.

In a recent development, “It’s a bit of a Rorschach test,” she notes. “Some people come out shaking, terrified. And I think some people are like, ‘Wow, what a good time!’ I also think that you have to hide the medicine in the food a little bit. I don’t think a purely doomsday story is going to reach many people.”.

In a recent development, UNDER PRESSURE “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film,” Garfield claims. “They didn’t kill it. They could have killed it.”.

In a recent development, garfield, meanwhile, may leave the film eternally bonded with Altman—the role that could help him finally clinch the Oscar. (Garfield’s been nominated twice but hasn’t won yet.) Before making Artificial, Garfield says, he had a positive impression of Altman. He seemed friendly, “like maybe we would’ve been buddies on the kibbutz.”.

As he dove deeper, though, Garfield’s feelings about Altman got stranger and more complicated in ways that the film addresses both head-on and obliquely. Is Altman someone who habitually tells tall tales? Uses lies to say what needs to be said, as Sam tells Ilya in the movie? Imagines anecdotes about waving to the A-lister who’s playing him in a biopic?

Whatever Altman’s relationship with reality is, the version of him we see in Artificial is charming, ingratiating, prone to grandiose hallucinations and to telling people exactly what they want to hear—then doing what he was going to do anyway. He’s not far off from an AGI approaching a real human consciousness, art imitating a machine imitating life.

Industry observers note that “There are certain threads that feel consistent, which is a questioning of his ability to tell or his commitment to the truth,” Garfield says. “How often is he telling the truth to himself? How often is he telling the truth to others? And how many versions of the truth are there, and how is he utilizing that in order to...”.

“Because I ultimately do believe that Sam feels, in our film and in life, that he is serving the good of mankind.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lawrence Sullivan, better known to the online world as the 'Florida Joker', is in GTA 6. After accusing Rockstar Games of using his likeness without consent and then demanding a $10m payout, the two parties have seemingly settled their differences.

Grand Theft Auto 6's earliest controversy came from its very first official trailer, when Sullivan alleged one of the teaser's similarly tattooed characters was modeled after him. The former tattoo model, who first went viral because of a mugshot that shared an uncanny resemblance to Batman's Joker, soon called on Rockstar to pay him $2m. His demand promptly shot up to $10m, before he dropped all legal threats and politely asked to officially work with the developer.

Rockstar seems to have relented to that last request - the vast GTA 6 credits include none other than one Lawrence Sullivan, listed under the 'Local Population' cast, alongside dozens of other names.

GTA 6 players wasted no time, and quickly found the suspect first teased way back in that original 2023 trailer. In its quest to parody all parts of modern life under capitalism, GTA 6 lets you doomscroll through a social media app called Snapmatic, which flings an endless number of short-form clips and thirst traps at you. If you're lucky enough, or if you scroll for long enough, you'll find a video of Sullivan's in-game counterpart beating up a fake lookalike. He certainly sounds like Sullivan, too.

According to recent reports, "Two years y'all been talking crazy about me," he wrote under a recent Instagram post. "Who got the last laugh now?!".

The GTA 6 credits were illuminating for other reasons, too. We finally know who voices the game's loveable duo, Jason and Lucia, for one. All 34 of the infamously fired Rockstar workers also appear in GTA 6's credits. The controversial move eventually led to accusations of union busting on Rockstar's part, which is right now being investigated as part of an employment tribunal in Scotland.

10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it.
  • In a recent development, with watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does.
  • Sources indicate that it seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest patch isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:.

In a recent development, with watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

Sources indicate that it seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

Sources indicate that while you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a significant fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the upcoming Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

Industry observers note that to use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Your Apple Watch's fresh Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

In a recent development, it seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Recent findings suggest that apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never revealed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

Now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

It has been revealed that siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

Industry observers note that the fresh Find My app on the Apple Watch indicates a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

Recent findings suggest that after opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

Recent findings suggest that while it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

The Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Recent findings suggest that low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

Recent findings suggest that the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that new arrivals are landing in the PlayStation Plus Game Catalog this month, but at the same time, you can also expect a few departures from that gaming library.
  • In a recent development, this month's biggest departure is Granblue Fantasy Relink, a massive fantasy game with a storybook art style, cinematic boss fights, and a large roster of characters who all possess unique abilities to master.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming arrivals are landing in the PlayStation Plus Game Catalog this month, but at the same time, you can also expect a few departures from that gaming library. Fortunately, the number of games leaving soon are on the smaller side, as there'll be only three exits in total. Unfortunately, one of those games that you're running out of time to play through the Game Catalog is a massive and pretty fun fantasy title, so get those hours in while you can. PlayStation Plus Game Catalog games leaving soon Granblue Fantasy Relink Granblue Fantasy Relink Somerville Fade to Silence This month's biggest departure is Granblue Fantasy Relink, a massive fantasy game with a storybook art style, cinematic boss fights, and a large roster of characters who all possess unique abilities to master. First released in February 2024, Granblue Fantasy Relink is built around real-time combat and flashy team-up mechanics, making for a visually striking experience overall. While the story isn't much to write home about, it's the gameplay and worldbuilding where this Granblue spin-off shines, and it got even better earlier this year with the Endless Ragnarok expansion. In comparison, Somerville is a story-rich puzzle game that's oozing atmosphere with its slick art direction, and Fade to Silence is a single-player and co-op survival-crafting adventure set in a post-apocalyptic world that is feeling the chill of an eternal winter. While the Game Catalog is going to be a little poorer without those three titles, it is getting some great games this month. Death Stranding 2: On the Beach is the headline act, and it'll be joined by several more titles like Atomfall, Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake, and Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii. All PlayStation Plus subscribers can also grab a trio of freebies between now and November 30: Dead Island 2, Tomb Raider 4-6 Remastered, and Monster Train 2.

After taking seven years to make Persona 6 and four years to make Persona 5, Atlus promises future games will come quicker

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Persona 6 is still slowly chugging in the background, but developer Atlus is promising that future games in its beloved RPG series won't take quite as long as they used to.
  • There was a four year gap between 2012's Persona 4 Golden and the original Persona 5, and it's already been seven years since the expanded Persona 5 Royal first dropped.
  • P-Studio general producer Kazuhisa Wada recently assured folks that the pattern wouldn't repeat again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Persona 6 is still slowly chugging in the background, but developer Atlus is promising that future games in its beloved RPG series won't take quite as long as they used to.

There was a four year gap between 2012's Persona 4 Golden and the original Persona 5, and it's already been seven years since the expanded Persona 5 Royal first dropped. Despite the sometimes agonising wait filled with countless spin-offs and collaborations with live service games, we've only seen a vague teaser trailer for the next proper Persona.

P-Studio general producer Kazuhisa Wada recently assured folks that the pattern wouldn't repeat again. "Persona 6 is not the end," he stated in a Sega Samania interview translated by GamesRadar. "We have been working to make sure that people won't have to wait as long for the next game as they have previously. In order for Persona to grow as an IP, we consider how to live up to people's expectations in terms of creativity and development every day.".

In a recent development, wada doesn't go into any more detail about how Atlus intends to release Persona games quicker. Is the next mainline game already in development alongside Persona 6, or is Atlus just streamlining how it makes games? Either way, the studio seems to have abandoned its divisive habit of returning to and improving its games after a few years - P3 Portable, P4 Golden, P5 Royal. I imagine that'll cut down on wait times, at least somewhat.

"Large-scale RPGs like the Persona series take five years or more to develop," he added. "So there can be a long time between numbered entries.".

Sources indicate that as for Persona 6 itself, Wada unsurprisingly "can't say much" about the much-hyped, high-schooling, demon-punching game. "But we want our games to demonstrate all of the hard work we've put in. With that in mind, we are creating something better than anything we've made before, and that is hugely satisfying.".

It has been revealed that we don't know much about Atlus' occult sequel, officially, but a massive information leak earlier in the year revealed a full achievement list for Persona 6 and a bunch of other unreleased games, including Kingdom Hearts 4 and an unannounced Sea of Thieves project. Be wary of online spoilers, then.

I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications.
  • Sources indicate that the massive AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe.
  • OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

Sources indicate that the massive AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Industry observers note that accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

It has been revealed that these ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly claims that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI states customers accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

In a recent development, gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health problems like eating disorders.

In a recent development, these protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

According to recent reports, as with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly promptly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

Recent findings suggest that if you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All consumers, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

In a recent development, apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

In a recent development, the new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

According to recent reports, if your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Owners must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft notes customers identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

According to recent reports, yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence.".

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires customers to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

According to recent reports, claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

It has been revealed that in terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide people towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic notes it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in a post to X, "The Everything App," US entertainment and communications conglomerate Comcast revealed that Grand Theft Auto 6's historic launch drove record-breaking internet traffic. According to Comcast, only a quarter of "the entire internet" was downloading Rockstar's latest cozy game phenomenon.

"GTA 6 didn't just break records in gaming," Comcast wrote. "Its launch drove the biggest internet traffic day in our network history, with traffic climbing 31% above an average day. At peak, GTA 6 accounted for nearly a quarter of all network traffic.".

In a recent development, comcast shared a video of a line graph showing the massive relative spike in activity on November 19. The chart is unlabeled except for the date, but it presumably corresponds to the volume of data being downloaded across Comcast's entire network.

And that last but does add a caveat to the numbers Comcast cited: Its network and "the entire internet" are two different things, unless I'm missing something here or Comcast's data accounts for other ISPs and other countries, not just its own services.

Regardless, it's still a significant bit of fun with statistics, another example of the totalizing footprint of what may be the largest commercial launch in entertainment history. Imagine how much bigger it would have been launching on PC as well.

💡 Key Takeaways
